title: Friends of other beliefs
hook: give a reason for your hope with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), and listen as well
tomorrow: work shows up in Eden before anything goes wrong. so is work a curse?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poor: a man at the gate with a name, Lazarus, honored and not just helped. Your line was not a project. Today, a friend with different answers to the big questions.
screen: `NOT A PROJECT.` → `A FRIEND WITH DIFFERENT ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The concert's over, the car's warm, and the friend in the passenger seat finally asks it: okay, but do you actually believe all of that? Acts has a story that starts in the same spot. Paul is in Athens, a city of temples and statues, and the people there want to hear what this new teaching is. So they bring him to speak. But before he does, Acts says, he has been walking the streets, looking closely at what they honor. On one altar he found words carved for a god nobody could name. So where does he start?
screen: `DO YOU ACTUALLY BELIEVE ALL THAT?` → `PAUL IN ATHENS, LOOKING.` → `AN ALTAR FOR A GOD NOBODY NAMED.`

segments.voice: He starts with their altar. In the King James Bible: “For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.” He looked before he spoke. Then he quotes their poets, not his own: “For in him we live, and move, and have our being.” And he tells them God “hath made of one blood all nations of men.” One blood: a single human family, named before any disagreement. Paul doesn't hide his own faith; he goes on to speak of Jesus and the resurrection. Acts is honest about how it went. Some mocked, and others said, “We will hear thee again of this matter.” The door stayed open. The First Letter of Peter puts the posture in one line: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear.” Someone asks first. The answer is about hope, not winning. The letter of James puts listening ahead of it all: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.” And Colossians wants words “alway with grace, seasoned with salt”: kind, and still honest. Gentleness and respect is that meekness and fear, in plainer English.
screen: `HE LOOKED BEFORE HE SPOKE.` · `HE QUOTED THEIR POETS.` · `OF ONE BLOOD, ALL NATIONS.` · `SWIFT TO HEAR, READY TO ANSWER.` · then, large: `GENTLENESS AND RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a friend whose beliefs differ from yours, or who holds none in particular. Write them one honest question about what gives them hope, and send it if it feels right. Then sit with their name, and let whatever they might answer be theirs, without drafting a reply.
Friends of other beliefs. People you love who see the big questions differently, met by looking and listening first, and with an honest answer when they ask.
Your line: gentleness and respect, the way Paul read their altar before he said a word. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1723 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 42 OF 70.` → `TOMORROW: WORK SHOWS UP IN EDEN BEFORE ANYTHING GOES WRONG. A CURSE?`

howItsDone: Christians talk about faith with friends of other beliefs in different ways; Paul's speech in Athens (Acts 17) and 1 Peter 3:15 are passages churches turn to for how to do it; churches take part in interfaith friendship and shared service in their own ways.

fork.setup: your lab partner is fasting for her holy month and mentions it while you're both starving before lunch. you've never asked about it. what does Athens suggest first?

fork.reveal: Paul looked closely at what Athens honored before he spoke. swift to hear comes first; your own answer can wait until she asks.

original.note: the Greek word the King James renders 'meekness' in 1 Peter 3:15: gentleness.

what it means: the answer is about hope, given when someone asks, with meekness and fear, after listening.
what a scholar hears: Peter's word for answer is apologia, a reasoned reply; in Athens Paul builds his on their altar and their own poets (Acts 17:23, 28).

chat.meaning: Paul looked before he spoke, and Peter's answer is about hope, given when asked, with meekness. Listening comes first.

notes: Day 1592 (A reason for hope) used 1 Peter 3:15 with the same carry; this day's angle is Paul in Athens (Acts 17) as the story, with the order of 1 Peter 3:15 (someone asks first) and the listening half (James 1:19; Colossians 4:6).
The carry 'gentleness and respect' is the index line; the KJV reads 'meekness and fear'. The lesson quotes the KJV and calls the carry the same posture in plainer English. Confirm.
Greek 'prautes' (1 Peter 3:15, prautetos) glossed 'gentleness'. Confirm spelling and pronunciation.
v3 story shape: the hook stops before Paul speaks; the teach answers with the altar (Acts 17:23). Acts 17 was last used on days 1517–1520 with a different angle.

Unity thread: Acts 17:26 'of one blood all nations of men' named as a single human family. Paul's own preaching of Jesus and the resurrection (17:31–32) is kept, so the story isn't flattened into 'all the same'. Acts 17:16 (his spirit 'stirred' by the idols) is not voiced; the lesson says only that he looked closely at what they honored (17:23 'beheld your devotions'). Confirm framing.

Acts 17:28: only the first clause is quoted; the 'certain also of your own poets' line is paraphrased ('he quotes their poets'), and the lesson treats both clauses as from their poets, as many readers do (Epimenides/Aratus). Confirm that 'he quotes their poets' fairly covers 17:28.
Trapdoor: apologia as the Greek of 'answer' in 1 Peter 3:15 is a lexicon fact; confirm.
Colossians named without an author ('Colossians wants words…').
Fork: the lab partner's 'holy month' is unnamed on purpose (no claim about any tradition's practice).
Grace, day 1 of the arc: after the choir concert Nia asks whether she actually believes all of it; Grace froze.
